citation.title: A Note on Close Elections and Regression Analysis of the Party Incumbency Advantage

standing_assumptions:
The paper (Statistics, Politics, and Policy 2014; 5(1-2): 1–11; printed and PDF page numbers coincide) states two propositions about estimators computed from a data set of elections indexed by pairs $it$ (region $i$, election $t$). Everything below was read from the page images.
[Model (1), Section 3.1, p. 5] “We now prove that a variant of the RD estimator is exactly reproduced by an OLS regression that includes all $N$ elections. Consider a statistical model that would motivate the use of the OLS estimator: $$DV_{i(t+1)}=\alpha+\beta DemWin_{it}+\sum_{j=1}^{J}\gamma_jX_{ijt}+u_{i(t+1)},\qquad(1)$$ where $DV_{i(t+1)}$ represents a dependent variable of interest in the $t+1^{th}$ election in region $i$, $DemWin_{it}$ is an indicator variable for whether or not the Democratic party won the $t^{th}$ election in region $i$, and $X_{ijt}$ represents one of $J$ control variables associated with election $t$ in region $i$.”
[Setting of Proposition 1, p. 5] “We now prove that, under suitable conditions, ordinary least squares estimation of the model in equation (1) will exactly reproduce the RD estimate, even if the model in equation (1) is not correct. Let $k$ (the bandwidth) be a number between 0 and 1. Supposing that only the Democratic and Republican parties contest each election, a set of sufficient conditions for estimator equality follow:”. The forcing variable is defined inside Condition 1 (p. 5): “$DemVot_{it}$ is the difference between Democratic and Republican vote share in election $t$ in region $i$.” Conditions 1–3 (p. 5) and the definitions of $\hat\tau_{RD}$ and $U_b$ (p. 6) are transcribed in full in P023-T11.
[Model (2), Section 3.2, p. 6] “We now consider OLS estimators of model (1) such that the control variables include a polynomial expansion of $DemVot_{it}$. We will demonstrate that such estimators will tend to approximate $\hat\tau_{RD}$ in large samples. Consider the special case of the model (1), $$DV_{i(t+1)}=\alpha+\beta DemWin_{it}+\sum_{j=1}^{J}\gamma_jDemVot_{it}^{j}+u_{i(t+1)}.\qquad(2)$$”
[Appendix B, p. 10] “Assume $$\mathrm{E}[DV\mid DemVot]=g(DemVot)\,\mathrm{I}[DemVot<0]+f(DemVot)\,\mathrm{I}[DemVot\ge0]$$ where $g()$ is continuous on $[-1,0)$ and $f()$ is continuous on $[0,1]$. Let $\alpha=\lim_{x\uparrow0}g(x)$ and $\beta=f(0)-\alpha$. Note that we have not assumed that $\beta$ has a causal interpretation.” Sampling, same page: “If the sample is drawn i.i.d. from a population $U$ with $\mathrm{Supp}(DemVot)\supseteq[-k,k]$, where $k>0$, then for large enough $N$, we have $\hat\beta_{OLS2}\approx\beta$.”
Not printed, and needed by a formal statement (each is the reading the validators used): (a) $DemVot_{it}\in[-1,1]$, a difference of two vote shares on the proportion scale: Appendix B works on $[-1,1]$ and the constant 1 in $J=2\lceil(1-k)/(2k)\rceil$ presupposes it. The Remark to Condition 3 and Section 4 give bandwidths in percentage points; 0.5 percentage points is $k=0.005$ (clarity note P023-N001). (b) Under the two-party supposition, $DemWin_{it}=1$ when $DemVot_{it}>0$ and $DemWin_{it}=0$ when $DemVot_{it}<0$. Section 3.1 states no convention for $DemVot_{it}=0$ (Appendix B writes $\mathrm{I}[DemVot\ge0]$); Proposition 1 does not depend on one, because $DemVot=0$ lies in the central bin. (c) The letter $J$ has three uses: the number of controls in (1); the value $2\lceil(1-k)/(2k)\rceil$ in Condition 2, the number of bin indicators; and the polynomial degree in (2). (d) $N$ is the number of pairs $it$ in the data, and $it\in U$ means that the pair $(i,t)$ belongs to the set $U$. (e) Nothing in Conditions 1–3 keeps a bin from being empty. The indicator of an empty bin is identically zero, so the OLS coefficient vector of (1) is then not unique, while the coefficient on $DemWin$ is the same in every least-squares solution; the factors $|\tilde U_j|^{-1}$ of Appendix A are to be read over non-empty bins only (clarity note P023-E006). (f) The definition of $\alpha$ presupposes that $g$ has a finite left limit at 0 (P023-A001, not confirmed as an error). (g) Both propositions concern the estimators $\hat\beta_{OLS}$, $\hat\beta_{OLS2}$ and $\hat\tau_{RD}$ as functions of the data, and $\beta$ of Appendix B is the jump of the conditional mean at 0; no potential-outcome model and no causal assumption is part of either statement.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 1, last paragraph (‘the resulting estimates rely solely on data from close elections’), and Section 3.2, last paragraph (‘will also only use information from close elections’), as printed; the witness is the validators’ construction (linear control) and is not in the paper
canonical_claim.statement:
Witness with a correctly specified linear control (validator's construction; not in the paper). Six elections with margins $x=(x_1,\dots,x_6)=(-\tfrac34,-\tfrac14,-\tfrac1{400},\tfrac1{400},\tfrac14,\tfrac34)$ (the values of $DemVot$) and $d_i=\mathrm{I}[x_i\ge0]$, so $d=(0,0,0,1,1,1)$ (the values of $DemWin$). Bandwidth $k=\tfrac1{200}$, so $U_b=\{i:-k<x_i\le k\}=\{3,4\}$ and Condition 1 holds. Outcomes $y_i=\tfrac12+\tfrac1{10}d_i+\tfrac1{20}x_i$, that is $y=(\tfrac{37}{80},\tfrac{39}{80},\tfrac{3999}{8000},\tfrac{4801}{8000},\tfrac{49}{80},\tfrac{51}{80})$, and $y'$ equal to $y$ except $y'_6=y_6+\tfrac1{100}=\tfrac{259}{400}$. For an outcome vector $z$ write $\hat\beta_{OLS2}(z)$ for the coefficient on $d$ in the OLS regression of $z$ on $(\mathbf 1,d,x)$, which is regression (2) with $J=1$; $\hat\tau_{RD}(z)$ for the difference in means over $U_b$; and $\hat\beta_{OLS}(z)$ for the coefficient on $d$ in the regression of Condition 2 with $k=\tfrac1{200}$.
Claims. (i) The matrix with columns $(\mathbf 1,d,x)$ has rank 3. (ii) $\hat\beta_{OLS2}(y)=\tfrac1{10}$; indeed $y$ satisfies (2) exactly with $\alpha=\tfrac12$, $\beta=\tfrac1{10}$, $\gamma_1=\tfrac1{20}$ and $u=0$. (iii) For every $z\in\mathbb R^6$, $\hat\beta_{OLS2}(z)=\sum_iw_iz_i$ with $w=\tfrac1{139202}(20299,\,-59901,\,-99600,\,99600,\,59901,\,-20299)$. (iv) $\hat\beta_{OLS2}(y')=\tfrac{1371721}{13920200}$, so $\hat\beta_{OLS2}(y')-\hat\beta_{OLS2}(y)=-\tfrac{20299}{13920200}\ne0$, although $y'_i=y_i$ for every $i\in U_b$ (the two vectors differ only at the margin $\tfrac34$). (v) $\hat\tau_{RD}(y)=\hat\tau_{RD}(y')=y_4-y_3=\tfrac{401}{4000}$. (vi) In Condition 2, $J=2\lceil(1-k)/(2k)\rceil=200$ and the six observations lie in bins $25,75,100,100,125,175$ (bin 100 is $(-k,k]$); the coefficient on $d$ is the same in every least-squares solution and $\hat\beta_{OLS}(y)=\hat\beta_{OLS}(y')=\tfrac{401}{4000}$. (vii) Consequence: the coefficient of the exactly specified polynomial regression (2) is not a function of the outcomes of the elections in $U_b$, while $\hat\tau_{RD}$ and the coarsened $\hat\beta_{OLS}$ are.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: From the paper: regression (2) (p. 6) with $J=1$, and $\hat\beta_{OLS2}$, “the OLS estimator of $\beta$ in (2)” (Proposition 2, p. 7); $\hat\tau_{RD}$ and $U_b\equiv\{it:-k<DemVot_{it}\le k\}$ (p. 6); Condition 2, $X_{ijt}=\mathrm{I}[2j-J-1<DemVot_{it}/k\le2j-J+1]$, $J=2\lceil\frac{1-k}{2k}\rceil$ (p. 5), with the reference bin $X_{i0t}=\mathrm{I}[-J-1\le DemVot_{it}/k\le-J+1]$ of Appendix A (p. 9). Formal reading of ‘rely solely on data from close elections’ and ‘only use information from close elections’ (the validators’; validated.json, P023-E001, natural_reading): with the margins held fixed, the estimate takes the same value on any two outcome vectors that agree on the elections in the close-election window $U_b$. Defined by the validator (P023-E001/v1/artifact/derivation.md, sections 1–2): the six-point design, the two outcome vectors, and the weights $w=r/(r^{\top}r)$ with $r$ the residual of $d$ on the columns $(\mathbf 1,x)$.
canonical_claim.note: Every number above was recomputed in exact rational arithmetic when this list was fixed and agrees with P023-E001/v1/artifact/exact_results.json (finite_linear) and check.out. In (vi) all bins but five are empty, so $\hat\beta_{OLS}$ is the coefficient on $d$ common to all least-squares solutions (standing assumption (e)); dropping the empty bins gives the same value. Both outcome vectors are possible realizations of one exactly specified model: with independent errors $U_i\in\{-\tfrac1{100},0,\tfrac1{100}\}$ of probabilities $\tfrac14,\tfrac12,\tfrac14$ and $Y_i=\tfrac12+\tfrac1{10}d_i+\tfrac1{20}x_i+U_i$, $y$ is the draw with all errors zero and $y'$ the draw with one positive error at $x=\tfrac34$ (derivation.md, section 4); that is context and not part of the target. All outcomes lie strictly between 0 and 1. The comparison does not say that the finite-window value $\tfrac{401}{4000}$ equals the jump $\tfrac1{10}$; it says that a distant change moves the polynomial coefficient and moves neither $\hat\tau_{RD}$ nor the coarsened coefficient. What a proof establishes: the statements on pp. 3 and 7 are false for a correctly specified linear control. It does not touch Proposition 1, the abstract, or the ‘may’ sentence on p. 8, which the coarsened estimator makes true. The second validator's independent artifact is P023-E001/v2/artifact/derivation.md.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 1, last paragraph, and Section 3.2, last paragraph, as printed (the same statements as P023-T1); the witness is the validators’ construction with the degree-7 control of estimator (c) and is not in the paper
canonical_claim.statement:
Witness with a correctly specified degree-7 control (validator's construction; not in the paper). Sixteen elections with margins $x_i\in\{\pm\tfrac18,\pm\tfrac28,\dots,\pm\tfrac88\}$ in increasing order, $x=(-8,-7,\dots,-1,1,\dots,7,8)/8$, and $d_i=\mathrm{I}[x_i>0]$. Bandwidth $k=\tfrac15$, so $U_b=\{i:-\tfrac15<x_i\le\tfrac15\}=\{8,9\}$ (the margins $-\tfrac18$ and $\tfrac18$) and Condition 1 holds. Outcomes $y_i=\tfrac12+\tfrac1{10}d_i+\tfrac1{20}x_i+\tfrac1{100}x_i^7$, and $y'$ equal to $y$ except at the margin 1: $y_{16}=\tfrac{33}{50}$, $y'_{16}=\tfrac{67}{100}$. $\hat\beta_{OLS2}(z)$ is the coefficient on $d$ in the OLS regression of $z$ on $(\mathbf 1,d,x,x^2,\dots,x^7)$, which is regression (2) with $J=7$; $\hat\tau_{RD}$ and $\hat\beta_{OLS}$ are as in P023-T1 with $k=\tfrac15$.
Claims. (i) The $16\times9$ matrix with columns $(\mathbf 1,d,x,\dots,x^7)$ has rank 9. (ii) $\hat\beta_{OLS2}(y)=\tfrac1{10}$; $y$ satisfies (2) exactly with $\alpha=\tfrac12$, $\beta=\tfrac1{10}$, $\gamma_1=\tfrac1{20}$, $\gamma_7=\tfrac1{100}$, the other $\gamma_j=0$, and $u=0$. (iii) For every $z\in\mathbb R^{16}$, $\hat\beta_{OLS2}(z)=\sum_iw_iz_i$ with $w=\tfrac1{1607}(-175,\,725,\,-685,\,-643,\,554,\,1289,\,239,\,-2911,\,2911,\,-239,\,-1289,\,-554,\,643,\,685,\,-725,\,175)$; every weight is non-zero. (iv) $\hat\beta_{OLS2}(y')=\tfrac{3249}{32140}$, so $\hat\beta_{OLS2}(y')-\hat\beta_{OLS2}(y)=\tfrac{7}{6428}\ne0$, although $y'_i=y_i$ for every $i\in U_b$. (v) $\hat\tau_{RD}(y)=\hat\tau_{RD}(y')=y_9-y_8=\tfrac{11796481}{104857600}$. (vi) In Condition 2, $J=2\lceil(1-k)/(2k)\rceil=4$, the bins are $[-1,-\tfrac35]$, $(-\tfrac35,-\tfrac15]$, $(-\tfrac15,\tfrac15]$, $(\tfrac15,\tfrac35]$, $(\tfrac35,1]$, the observations lie in bins $(0,0,0,0,1,1,1,2,2,3,3,3,4,4,4,4)$, and $\hat\beta_{OLS}(y)=\hat\beta_{OLS}(y')=\tfrac{11796481}{104857600}$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: As for P023-T1, with regression (2) at $J=7$, the degree of estimator (c) of Section 4 (p. 7: “Estimator (c) includes a degree 7 polynomial expansion of $DemVot_{it}$”). Defined by the validator (P023-E001/v1/artifact/derivation.md, section 3): the sixteen-point design, the two outcome vectors and the weights $w=r/(r^{\top}r)$ with $r$ the residual of $d$ on the columns $(\mathbf 1,x,\dots,x^7)$.
canonical_claim.note: Recomputed in exact rational arithmetic when this list was fixed; agrees with exact_results.json (finite_degree7) and check.out. The baseline is exactly of degree 7 with a non-zero seventh-degree coefficient, so no further polynomial term can improve its fit; the same two-realization remark as in P023-T1 applies (derivation.md, section 4). The window $k=\tfrac15$ is wide; it is a valid bandwidth under the paper's conditions and was chosen by the validator to keep the design simple, and P023-T1 uses the narrow window $k=\tfrac1{200}$. A Lean proof can avoid inverting a $9\times9$ matrix: it suffices to check that $w$ lies in the column space of $(\mathbf 1,d,x,\dots,x^7)$, is orthogonal to the eight polynomial columns and has $w^{\top}d=1$. All outcomes lie strictly between 0 and 1 ($\tfrac{11}{25}\le y_i\le\tfrac{67}{100}$).

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 1, last paragraph (p. 3), and Section 3.2, last paragraph (p. 7), as repaired by Sol: sole reliance on close-election outcomes is reserved for the coarsened regression of Proposition 1; for polynomial controls, a common discontinuity target together with non-zero weights on distant outcomes
canonical_claim.location: p. 3 (PDF p. 3) and p. 7 (PDF p. 7); the ‘may’ sentence of Section 5, p. 8 (PDF p. 8), is kept
canonical_claim.statement:
Sol's corrected text (validated.json, P023-E001, prior_correction.corrected_text), verbatim: “For the coarsened specification, full-sample OLS exactly reproduces the specified close-election RD estimate. Under a correctly specified polynomial conditional mean, the polynomial OLS coefficient estimates the same cutoff discontinuity as the limiting RD estimator, while outcomes outside the close-election window also enter its estimation. A shared cutoff target alone does not imply equal observation weights, sampling variance, or finite-sample bias. Its causal interpretation and scope require the appropriate assumptions.”
Mathematical content, written out (validator's derivation, P023-E001/v1/artifact/derivation.md, sections 1, 5, 6 and 7). Data: $N$ elections with margins $x_i\in[-1,1]$, indicators $d_i\in\{0,1\}$ with $d_i=1$ if $x_i>0$ and $d_i=0$ if $x_i<0$, and outcomes $y_i\in\mathbb R$; $k\in(0,1)$; $U_b=\{i:-k<x_i\le k\}$.
(a) [Coarsened regression: exact localization.] Suppose $U_b$ contains $n_1\ge1$ observations with $d_i=1$ and $n_0\ge1$ with $d_i=0$ (Condition 1 implies this). Let $\hat\beta_{OLS}$ be the coefficient on $d$ in a least-squares fit of $y$ on an intercept, $d$ and the bin indicators of Condition 2. Then $\hat\beta_{OLS}$ is the same in every least-squares solution, and $\hat\beta_{OLS}=\sum_iw^{c}_iy_i$ with $w^{c}_i=1/n_1$ for $i\in U_b$ with $d_i=1$, $w^{c}_i=-1/n_0$ for $i\in U_b$ with $d_i=0$, and $w^{c}_i=0$ for $i\notin U_b$. Hence $\hat\beta_{OLS}=\hat\tau_{RD}$, and two outcome vectors that agree on $U_b$ give the same $\hat\beta_{OLS}$.
(b) [Polynomial regression: the weights.] Fix $J\ge1$, let $Z$ be the $N\times(J+1)$ matrix with rows $(1,x_i,\dots,x_i^{J})$, and suppose $[Z,d]$ has full column rank $J+2$. Put $r=d-Z(Z^{\top}Z)^{-1}Z^{\top}d$. Then $Z^{\top}r=0$, $r^{\top}d=r^{\top}r>0$, and the OLS coefficient on $d$ in the regression (2) of $y$ on $[Z,d]$ is $\hat\beta_{OLS2}=r^{\top}y/r^{\top}r=\sum_iw_iy_i$ with $w_i=r_i/(r^{\top}r)$; moreover $\sum_iw_i=0$, $\sum_iw_ix_i^{j}=0$ for $j=1,\dots,J$, and $\sum_iw_id_i=1$. Changing one outcome $y_i$ by $\delta$, and no other, changes $\hat\beta_{OLS2}$ by exactly $w_i\delta$.
(c) [Polynomial regression: no exact localization.] In (b), suppose also that at least one $d_i=1$ and at least one $d_i=0$. Then the number of distinct non-zero margin values $x_i$ with $w_i=0$ is at most $2J$ (at most $J$ negative and at most $J$ positive). Consequently, if more than $2J$ distinct non-zero margin values lie outside $(-k,k]$, there are an observation $i\notin U_b$ and outcome vectors $y,y'$ that differ only at $i$, so agree on $U_b$, with $\hat\beta_{OLS2}(y)\ne\hat\beta_{OLS2}(y')$, while $\hat\tau_{RD}(y)=\hat\tau_{RD}(y')$ and, under the hypothesis of (a), $\hat\beta_{OLS}(y)=\hat\beta_{OLS}(y')$.
(d) [Common target under exact polynomial specification.] In (b), suppose the outcomes are random with $\mathrm E[y_i\mid x_1,\dots,x_N]=\alpha+\beta d_i+\sum_{j=1}^{J}\gamma_jx_i^{j}$ for every $i$. Then $\mathrm E[\hat\beta_{OLS2}\mid x_1,\dots,x_N]=\beta$. If, given the margins, the errors $u_i=y_i-\mathrm E[y_i\mid x_1,\dots,x_N]$ are uncorrelated with variances $\sigma_i^2$, then $\mathrm{Var}(\hat\beta_{OLS2}\mid x_1,\dots,x_N)=\sum_iw_i^2\sigma_i^2$, to which every observation with $w_i\ne0$ and $\sigma_i^2>0$ contributes a positive amount, whether or not it lies in $U_b$.
(e) [Population illustration, uniform margins.] Let $X$ be uniform on $[-1,1]$, $D=\mathrm I[X\ge0]$, $p_J$ the $L^2$ projection of $D$ on $\mathrm{span}(1,X,\dots,X^J)$, $r_J=D-p_J$ and $v_J=\mathrm E[r_J^2]$. Then $p_1(x)=\tfrac12+\tfrac34x$, $v_1=\tfrac1{16}$, $r_1(\tfrac9{10})/v_1=-\tfrac{14}5$ and $\mathrm E[r_1^2\,\mathrm I(|X|\ge\tfrac12)]/v_1=\tfrac18$; and $p_7(x)=\tfrac12+(11025x-40425x^3+63063x^5-32175x^7)/4096$, $v_7=\tfrac{1225}{65536}$, $r_7(\tfrac9{10})/v_7=-\tfrac{20283449}{6125000}$ and $\mathrm E[r_7^2\,\mathrm I(|X|\ge\tfrac12)]/v_7=\tfrac{572158921}{10276044800}$. If $\mathrm E[Y\mid X]=\tfrac12+\tfrac1{10}D+\tfrac1{20}X$ (for $J=1$), respectively $\tfrac12+\tfrac1{10}D+\tfrac1{20}X+\tfrac1{100}X^7$ (for $J=7$), then the population OLS coefficient on $D$, $\mathrm E[r_JY]/v_J$, equals $\tfrac1{10}$, and the population RD difference $\mathrm E[Y\mid0<X\le k]-\mathrm E[Y\mid-k<X<0]$ equals $\tfrac1{10}+\tfrac k{20}$, respectively $\tfrac1{10}+\tfrac k{20}+\tfrac{k^7}{400}$, which tends to $\tfrac1{10}$ as $k\to0$: one target, and a strictly positive share of the OLS influence variance on $|X|\ge\tfrac12$.
(f) [Accepted 19 October shared-consistency qualification.] For every fixed tolerance ε>0, P(|A_N-B_N|>ε) ≤ P(|A_N-β|>ε/2)+P(|B_N-β|>ε/2). Consequently, if the actual polynomial OLS and shrinking-window RD estimators are both consistent in probability for β, their difference tends to zero in probability. No independence between them is required. The two consistency statements are explicit hypotheses, not conclusions of exact specification alone.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: From the paper: Conditions 1–3, $U_b$, $\hat\tau_{RD}$ and $\hat\beta_{OLS}$ (pp. 5–6; transcribed in P023-T11); regression (2) and $\hat\beta_{OLS2}$ (pp. 6–7). The printed sentences being replaced are transcribed in P023-T10. Defined by the validator (derivation.md, sections 1 and 5): the finite-sample residual $r$ and weights $w$; the population projection $p_J$, residual $r_J$ and $v_J$; and the influence-variance share $\mathrm E[r_J^2\,\mathrm I(|X|\ge\tfrac12)]/v_J$ (under an exactly specified mean with independent homoskedastic errors $U$ the influence function of the OLS coefficient is $r_J(X)U/v_J$).
canonical_claim.note: Part (a) is Proposition 1 (P023-T11) in weight form and should reuse it. Parts (b)–(d) are exact finite-sample linear algebra for every $J$; they are the formal content of ‘outcomes outside the close-election window also enter its estimation’ and of ‘estimates the same cutoff discontinuity’. In (c) the validator states the count for a design with distinct margins (derivation.md, section 6: ‘Apart from at most 2J distinct margins, residuals and hence outcome weights are nonzero’); counting distinct non-zero margin values, as here, is the same argument and also covers repeated margins and a tie at 0. The argument: the fitted polynomial $p_J$ with coefficients $(Z^{\top}Z)^{-1}Z^{\top}d$ is neither the zero polynomial nor the constant 1, because its fitted values sum to $\sum_id_i\in[1,N-1]$; so $p_J$ vanishes at no more than $J$ negative margins and $p_J-1$ at no more than $J$ positive margins. Part (e) was recomputed exactly when this list was fixed (exact_results.json, population_degree1 and population_degree7). ‘The limiting RD estimator’ in the corrected text refers to consistency of $\hat\tau_{RD}$ for the jump as $k\to0$ and $Nk\to\infty$, which is part of P023-T8 and is not repeated here; a common target under merely approximate specification is the subject of P023-E002 (P023-T7, P023-T8). The last two sentences of the corrected text are a non-implication and a caution about interpretation: their formal content is that the weights of (a) and of (b) differ in designs where both estimators have the same target (P023-T1, P023-T2 and (e)). No claim is made that two estimators with one target differ in causal scope or in external validity. The artifact's comparison of leading noise variances ($16\sigma^2/N$ and $(65536/1225)\sigma^2/N$ against $4\sigma^2/(Nk)$) is a leading-order remark and is not a target. The accepted review's shared-consistency implication is now formalized separately in P023_Review.polynomial_rd_shared_consistency, using the actual estimator definitions and a finite ε/2 union bound. This does not finish the broader regularity theorem T8.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Remark to Proposition 2 (‘we require that the model fit cannot be meaningfully improved by including additional terms’), read with Appendix B (‘$\mathrm E[u|DemVot]\approx0$ and therefore $\mathrm E[\hat\beta_{OLS2}]\approx\beta$’), as printed; the witness (uniform margins, degrees 1 and 7) is the settling validator's construction and is not in the paper
canonical_claim.statement:
Witness with one fixed, regular margin distribution (settling validator's construction; not in the paper). Let $X$ ($=DemVot$) be uniform on $[-1,1]$ and $D=\mathrm I[X\ge0]$ ($=DemWin$). For $a>0$ and $0<\eta\le1$ let $h_\eta(x)=a\cdot\mathrm{clip}(x/\eta,-1,1)$, that is $h_\eta(x)=ax/\eta$ for $|x|\le\eta$ and $a\,\mathrm{sign}(x)$ otherwise, and $Y=\tfrac12+h_\eta(X)+U$ with $U=\pm\tfrac1{10}$ equiprobable and independent of $X$. For $J\ge1$ let $q_J$ be the $L^2$ projection of $D$ on $\mathrm{span}(1,X,\dots,X^J)$, $r_J=D-q_J$, $v_J=\mathrm E[r_J^2]$, and $b_J=\mathrm E[r_JY]/v_J$, the population coefficient on $D$ in the least-squares regression of $Y$ on $(1,D,X,\dots,X^J)$ (the probability limit of $\hat\beta_{OLS2}$ at fixed $J$).
Claims. (i) $h_\eta$ is continuous, odd and $(a/\eta)$-Lipschitz with $h_\eta(0)=0$, and $\mathrm E[Y\mid X]=\tfrac12+h_\eta(X)$ is continuous on $[-1,1]$; so Appendix B's assumptions hold with $g$ and $f$ the restrictions of $\tfrac12+h_\eta$, $\alpha=\tfrac12$ and $\beta=f(0)-\alpha=0$. (ii) The population RD difference $\tau_k=\mathrm E[Y\mid0<X\le k]-\mathrm E[Y\mid-k<X<0]$ equals $ak/\eta$ for $0<k\le\eta$, so $\tau_k\to0=\beta$ as $k\to0$. (iii) $r_1(x)=\tfrac12-\tfrac34x$ for $x>0$ and $v_1=\tfrac1{16}$; $r_7(x)=\tfrac12-(11025x-40425x^3+63063x^5-32175x^7)/4096$ for $x>0$ and $v_7=\tfrac{1225}{65536}$; $r_J(-x)=-r_J(x)$ for $x\ne0$. (iv) $b_J-\beta=2a-\dfrac a{v_J}\displaystyle\int_0^{\eta}r_J(x)\Big(1-\frac x\eta\Big)dx$. Hence $b_1=2a(1-\eta)^2$, and for $a=\tfrac1{20}$, $b_7=\tfrac1{10}-\tfrac{4096}{6125}\eta+\tfrac65\eta^2-\tfrac{33}{25}\eta^4+\tfrac{858}{875}\eta^6-\tfrac{143}{490}\eta^8$. At $a=\tfrac1{20}$, $\eta=\tfrac1{10000}$: $b_1=\tfrac{99980001}{1000000000}$ and $b_7=\tfrac{4896723787999993532000048047999857}{49000000000000000000000000000000000}$, that is 9.998 and 9.993 percentage points of vote share, with $\beta=0$ and $Y\in[\tfrac7{20},\tfrac{13}{20}]$. (v) [Fit.] The predictor $\tfrac12+a(2D-1)$ lies in the span of $(1,D)$, hence of the regressors of (2) at every degree, and $\mathrm E[(h_\eta(X)-a(2D-1))^2]=a^2\eta/3$. So the population mean squared error of the fitted regression (2), at any degree, exceeds the irreducible $\mathrm E[\mathrm{Var}(Y\mid X)]=\tfrac1{100}$ by at most $a^2\eta/3$, and no additional function of $X$, polynomial or not, can lower it by more than $a^2\eta/3$; at $a=\tfrac1{20}$, $\eta=\tfrac1{10000}$ this is $\tfrac1{12000000}$, at most $\tfrac1{120000}$ of the current mean squared error. (vi) For fixed $J$ and $a$, $b_J\to2a$ as $\eta\downarrow0$, while the bound in (v) tends to 0.

canonical_claim.statement:
Counterexample to ‘$J$ sufficiently large’ under continuity alone, with one fixed law and one fixed conditional mean (settling validator's construction; not in the paper). Let $X$ be uniform on $[-1,1]$, $D=\mathrm I[X\ge0]$, and for $J\ge1$ let $q_J$ be the $L^2$ projection of $D$ on $\mathrm{span}(1,X,\dots,X^J)$, $r_J=D-q_J$, $v_J=\mathrm E[r_J^2]$, $\kappa_J=\mathrm E|r_J|/v_J$ and, for bounded measurable $h$, $T_Jh=\mathrm E[r_Jh(X)]/v_J$.
Claims. (i) [Unbounded amplification.] $\kappa_J\to\infty$ as $J\to\infty$; precisely $\kappa_J=\tfrac4\pi\log J+O(1)$. (ii) [Norm.] For every $J$, $\sup\{T_Jh:\ h\text{ continuous on }[-1,1],\ h(0)=0,\ \sup|h|\le1\}=\kappa_J$. (iii) [One fixed $h$.] There exist a continuous $h:[-1,1]\to\mathbb R$ with $h(0)=0$ and $\sup|h|\le\tfrac1{12}$, and integers $J_1<J_2<\cdots$, such that $T_{J_m}h\ge m/4$ for every $m\ge1$. (iv) [Consequence.] Let $Y=\tfrac12+h(X)$ with this $h$. Then $\mathrm E[Y\mid X]=\tfrac12+h(X)$ is continuous, $Y\in[\tfrac5{12},\tfrac7{12}]$, Appendix B's assumptions hold with $g$, $f$ the restrictions of $\tfrac12+h$, $\alpha=\tfrac12$ and $\beta=f(0)-\alpha=0$, and the population coefficient on $D$ in the least-squares regression of $Y$ on $(1,D,X,\dots,X^J)$ is $b_J=T_Jh$. Hence $b_{J_m}\ge m/4$ for all $m$, $\limsup_{J\to\infty}b_J=+\infty$, and $b_J$ does not converge to $\beta=0$; while the population RD difference $\mathrm E[Y\mid0<X\le k]-\mathrm E[Y\mid-k<X<0]\to0$ as $k\to0$. (v) No such $h$ is Lipschitz (by P023-T8(c)).

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Appendix B, the step ‘$\mathrm E[u|DemVot]\approx0$ and therefore $\mathrm E[\hat\beta_{OLS2}]\approx\beta$’, and the Remark to Proposition 2, as repaired by Sol: the exact identity for the coefficient error and its bounds
canonical_claim.statement:
Sol's repair (validated.json, P023-E002, smallest_repair), first sentence and the sentence on a fixed degree, verbatim: “Replace the Appendix B inference by b_J-beta=E[r_J(h-p_J)]/v_J, with |b_J-beta|<=kappa_J||h-p_J||_infinity and <=||h-p_J||_2/sqrt(v_J). … For a claimed fixed-degree tolerance t, separately require |E[r_Jh]|/v_J<=t, or sufficiently kappa_J times the smooth-part uniform polynomial error <=t; replace negligible additional fitted-model MSE gain as a sufficient criterion.”
Written out in full. Let $(X,Y)$ be random variables with $X\in[-1,1]$ ($=DemVot$), $D=\mathrm I[X\ge0]$ ($=DemWin$), $\mathrm E[Y^2]<\infty$ and $\mathrm E[Y\mid X]=\alpha+\beta D+h(X)$ with $h$ bounded and measurable. Fix $J\ge1$, let $\mathcal P_J=\mathrm{span}(1,X,\dots,X^J)\subset L^2(P_X)$, $q_J$ the $L^2$ projection of $D$ on $\mathcal P_J$, $r_J=D-q_J$ and $v_J=\mathrm E[r_J^2]$. Assume the second-moment matrix of $(1,D,X,\dots,X^J)$ is positive definite, so $v_J>0$, and let $b_J$ be the coefficient on $D$ in the population least-squares regression of $Y$ on $(1,D,X,\dots,X^J)$.
(a) $\mathrm E[r_Jp(X)]=0$ for every polynomial $p$ of degree at most $J$; $\mathrm E[r_J]=0$; $\mathrm E[r_JD]=v_J$; and $b_J=\mathrm E[r_JY]/v_J$.
(b) [Identity.] $b_J-\beta=\dfrac{\mathrm E[r_Jh(X)]}{v_J}=\dfrac{\mathrm E[r_J\{h(X)-p(X)\}]}{v_J}$ for every polynomial $p$ of degree at most $J$.
(c) [Bounds.] With $\kappa_J=\mathrm E|r_J|/v_J$, $|b_J-\beta|\le\kappa_J\,\sup_x|h(x)-p(x)|$ and $|b_J-\beta|\le\|h-p\|_{L^2(P_X)}/\sqrt{v_J}$ for every such $p$.
(d) $\kappa_J\ge2$.
(e) [Exact specification.] If $h(X)=\sum_{j=1}^{J}\gamma_jX^j$ almost surely, then $b_J=\beta$.
(f) [Fixed-degree criterion replacing the Remark.] For $t>0$: $|b_J-\beta|\le t$ if and only if $|\mathrm E[r_Jh(X)]|\le t\,v_J$; it holds whenever $\kappa_J\inf_{\deg p\le J}\sup_x|h(x)-p(x)|\le t$, and whenever $\inf_{\deg p\le J}\|h-p\|_{L^2(P_X)}\le t\sqrt{v_J}$.
(g) [Finite sample.] Let $x_1,\dots,x_N\in[-1,1]$, $d_i=\mathrm I[x_i\ge0]$, let the matrix with rows $(1,d_i,x_i,\dots,x_i^J)$ have full column rank, and let $\tilde d$ be the least-squares residual of $d$ on the columns $(1,x,\dots,x^J)$. Then $\sum_i\tilde d_id_i=\sum_i\tilde d_i^2>0$ and $\hat\beta_{OLS2}=\sum_i\tilde d_iy_i/\sum_i\tilde d_i^2$; and if $\mathrm E[y_i\mid x_1,\dots,x_N]=\alpha+\beta d_i+h(x_i)$ for every $i$, then $$\mathrm E[\hat\beta_{OLS2}\mid x_1,\dots,x_N]-\beta=\frac{\sum_i\tilde d_ih(x_i)}{\sum_i\tilde d_i^2}.$$
(h) [Constants for uniform margins.] If $X$ is uniform on $[-1,1]$: $v_J=c_n^2/4$ with $n=\lfloor(J+1)/2\rfloor$ and $c_n=\binom{2n}{n}/4^n$. For $J=1$: $r_1(x)=\tfrac12-\tfrac34x$ for $x>0$, $v_1=\tfrac1{16}$, $\mathrm E|r_1|=\tfrac5{24}$, $\kappa_1=\tfrac{10}3$, $1/\sqrt{v_1}=4$. For $J=7$: $v_7=\tfrac{1225}{65536}$, $1/\sqrt{v_7}=\tfrac{256}{35}$ and $4.7642006857252250<\kappa_7<4.7642006857252260$.

canonical_claim.statement:

(2) [Section 3, (6)] for $X$ uniform on $[-1,1]$, $v_J^{\mathrm{unif}}=c_n^2/4$ with $n=\lfloor(J+1)/2\rfloor$, $c_n=\binom{2n}{n}/4^n$, and $c_n^2\ge1/(4n)$ for $n\ge1$. (3) [Section 4, (8)] under (H2), for every polynomial $p$ of degree at most $J$, $\mathrm E[(D-p(X))^2]\ge c\int_{-\delta}^{\delta}(\mathrm I[x\ge0]-p(x))^2dx$, whence $v_J\ge2c\delta\,v_J^{\mathrm{unif}}=c\delta c_n^2/2\ge c\delta/(8n)\ge c\delta/(4(J+1))$. (4) [Section 4, (9)] with $H(\theta)=h(\cos\theta)$ and $s=\lfloor J/2\rfloor+1$, $\frac1{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}|t|K_s(t)dt\le K/s$, so the convolution $H*K_s$ is a polynomial in $\cos\theta$ of degree at most $2s-2\le J$ within $KL/s$ of $H$; subtracting its value at 0 at most doubles the error because $h(0)=0$, giving $4KL/(J+1)$. (5) [Section 8] $\tau_k=\beta+\mathrm E[h(X)\mid0<X\le k]-\mathrm E[h(X)\mid-k<X<0]$; each side of the window has probability at least $ck$ for $k\le\delta$; a binomial count $n_s$ with mean $Np_s$ satisfies $P(n_s<Np_s/2)\le4/(Np_s)$. (6) [Section 8, before (24)] with $K_J=J+2$ and $M=\mathrm E[Y^2]$: $\mathrm E\|\hat G_J-G_J\|_F^2\le K_J^2/N$, $\mathrm E\|\hat t_J-t_J\|^2\le K_JM/N$, $\lambda_J\|c_J\|^2\le M$, and on the event $\|\hat G_J-G_J\|_{op}\le\lambda_J/2$, $\|\hat c_J-c_J\|\le\frac2{\lambda_J}\big[\|\hat t_J-t_J\|+\|\hat G_J-G_J\|_{op}\sqrt{M/\lambda_J}\big]$. Printed in the paper and still used: the representation $\mathrm E[DV\mid DemVot]=\alpha+\beta\,\mathrm I[DemVot\ge0]+h(DemVot)$ with $h(0)=0$ (p. 10).
canonical_claim.note: This is the repair that the rating adopts for Proposition 2 itself (repair cost: a minor regularity condition; ratings.json, P023-E002, doubt_settled: ‘b_J tends to beta at rate J^(-1/2) when the density is bounded below near the cutoff and h is Lipschitz’). The constant is deliberately not optimal; what matters is the rate, and a formalization that proves (c) with another explicit absolute constant is faithful to it. (H2) asks for a density bounded below only near the cutoff: no upper bound on the density is used, and the law may have atoms away from $[-\delta,\delta]$. (H4) holds automatically when $Y$ is a vote share in $[0,1]$. Continuity of $h$ alone is not enough (P023-T6), so the Lipschitz condition, or some other quantitative smoothness, is a real addition to the printed assumptions. The statement does not say that $J=1$ or $J=7$ is ‘sufficiently large’ in any application: at a fixed degree the coefficient error is governed by P023-T7(b)–(f), and the settling validator records that the adequacy of the linear and degree-7 controls of Table 1 cannot be determined from the paper. The bound in (b) and the kernel moment bound were re-derived by hand when this list was fixed.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Appendix A, proof of Proposition 1: the display after ‘Therefore,’, with the summation index corrected from $i\in U_b$ to $it\in U_b$
canonical_claim.statement:
As printed (p. 9): “When $DemWin_{it}=0$ or $DemWin_{it}=1$ for all $it\in\tilde U_j$, $Dem\ddot{W}in_{it}=0$. Therefore, $\hat\beta_{OLS}=(\sum_{i\in U_b}Dem\ddot{W}in_{it}^{2})^{-1}(\sum_{i\in U_b}Dem\ddot{W}in_{it}\,D\ddot{V}_{i(t+1)})$, the least squares estimator as applied only to observations in the interval covering the discontinuity (noting that $U_b=\tilde U_{J/2}$).”
Corrected (Sol's smallest_repair: “Write $\sum_{it\in U_b}$ in both sums.”), with every hypothesis. Let the data be a finite set of pairs $it$ with $DemVot_{it}\in[-1,1]$, $DemWin_{it}\in\{0,1\}$, $DemWin_{it}=1$ if $DemVot_{it}>0$ and $DemWin_{it}=0$ if $DemVot_{it}<0$, and $DV_{i(t+1)}\in\mathbb R$. Let $0<k<1$, $J=2\lceil\frac{1-k}{2k}\rceil$, $X_{ijt}=\mathrm I[2j-J-1<DemVot_{it}/k\le2j-J+1]$ for $j=1,\dots,J$, $X_{i0t}=\mathrm I[-J-1\le DemVot_{it}/k\le-J+1]$, $\tilde U_j\equiv\{it:X_{ijt}=1\}$ and $U_b\equiv\{it:-k<DemVot_{it}\le k\}$. For $it\in\tilde U_j$ put $$Dem\ddot{W}in_{it}\equiv DemWin_{it}-|\tilde U_j|^{-1}\sum_{i't'\in\tilde U_j}DemWin_{i't'},\qquad D\ddot{V}_{i(t+1)}\equiv DV_{i(t+1)}-|\tilde U_j|^{-1}\sum_{i't'\in\tilde U_j}DV_{i'(t'+1)}$$ (the printed definitions, each pair lying in exactly one $\tilde U_j$). Assume Condition 1, and let $\hat\beta_{OLS}$ be the coefficient on $DemWin$ of Condition 2. Then: (i) the sets $\tilde U_0,\dots,\tilde U_J$ partition the data and $U_b=\tilde U_{J/2}$; (ii) $Dem\ddot{W}in_{it}=0$ for every $it\notin U_b$; (iii) $\sum_{it\in U_b}Dem\ddot{W}in_{it}^{2}>0$ and $$\hat\beta_{OLS}=\Big(\sum_{it\in U_b}Dem\ddot{W}in_{it}^{2}\Big)^{-1}\Big(\sum_{it\in U_b}Dem\ddot{W}in_{it}\,D\ddot{V}_{i(t+1)}\Big),$$ both sums running over the pairs $(i,t)$ in $U_b$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: All from Appendix A, p. 9: “Let $X_{i0t}=\mathrm I[-J-1\le DemVot_{it}/k\le-J+1]$. By Wooldridge (2002: p. 579), $$\hat\beta_{OLS}=\Big(N^{-1}\sum_{j=0}^{J}\sum_{it\in\tilde U_j}Dem\ddot{W}in_{it}^{2}\Big)^{-1}\Big(N^{-1}\sum_{j=0}^{J}\sum_{it\in\tilde U_j}Dem\ddot{W}in_{it}\,D\ddot{V}_{i(t+1)}\Big),$$ where $Dem\ddot{W}in_{it}\equiv DemWin_{it}-\sum_{j=0}^{J}[X_{ijt}|\tilde U_j|^{-1}\sum_{i't'\in\tilde U_j}DemWin_{i't'}]$, $D\ddot{V}_{i(t+1)}\equiv DV_{i(t+1)}-\sum_{j=0}^{J}[X_{ijt}|\tilde U_j|^{-1}\sum_{i't'\in\tilde U_j}DV_{i'(t'+1)}]$ and $\tilde U_j\equiv\{it:X_{ijt}=1\}$.” Conditions 1 and 2 (p. 5) and $U_b$ (p. 6) are transcribed in P023-T11. In the print the double dot stands over the W of DemWin and the V of DV.
canonical_claim.note: A Minor misprint (the rating: ‘two sums in Appendix A are indexed by i where the set $U_b$ consists of (i,t) pairs’), included because the author asks for a formalization of the corrected version of every mathematical error. The validator's verdict is in _batch/P023-B01/verdicts.json (page check, with the crop work/page-09-proof-detail.png); the derivation of this step is the Appendix A paragraph of work/derivations.txt: in the central bin the residual of DemWin is $D-p$ with $p=n_1/n$, $\sum_{U_b}(D-p)^2=n_1n_0/n>0$ and $\sum_{U_b}(D-p)(y-\bar y_{U_b})=(n_1n_0/n)(\bar y_1-\bar y_0)$. The misprinted index was read on the page image when this list was fixed: both sums in this display read $i\in U_b$, and the display two lines below and the one on p. 6 read $it\in U_b$. The demeaning formulas are written here for the bin containing $it$, which equals the printed sum over $j$ whenever every bin is non-empty; for an empty bin the printed $|\tilde U_j|^{-1}$ is undefined and the term is to be omitted (standing assumption (e); clarity note P023-E006), and $\hat\beta_{OLS}$ is the coefficient on DemWin common to all least-squares solutions. The rating records no headline claim as affected; the display belongs to the proof of the result behind P023-H1.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 1, last paragraph (‘all flexibly specified … mathematically equivalent to studies of close elections’; ‘rely solely on data from close elections’), with Section 3.2, last paragraph, and Section 5, first two sentences, as printed
canonical_claim.location: p. 3 (PDF p. 3); p. 7 (PDF p. 7); p. 8 (PDF p. 8)
canonical_claim.statement:
Section 1 (p. 3): “In fact, we demonstrate that all flexibly specified empirical studies of the party incumbency advantage using ordinary least squares (OLS) regression are mathematically equivalent to studies of close elections. The mechanics of linear regression with a covariate control for vote share are such that the resulting estimates rely solely on data from close elections. It follows that any concerns about the study of close elections are equally applicable to regression analyses including the entire dataset of all elections. As a consequence, we argue that a focus on close elections is fundamental to the empirical study of the party incumbency advantage.”
Section 3.2, last paragraph (p. 7): “Thus, we have established that, under a variety of circumstances resembling real-world practice, the OLS estimator (as applied to the entire dataset) may either exactly reproduce or approximate the RD estimator of the party incumbency advantage. Since the RD estimator only uses information from close elections to estimate causal effects, it is also generally the case that the OLS estimator, when well-specified, will also only use information from close elections to estimate causal effects.”
Section 5 (p. 8): “We have demonstrated that OLS estimation of the party incumbency advantage may produce estimates that rely solely on data from close elections. The limitations of studying close elections to estimate causal effects – both in terms of bias and of external validity – are therefore equally applicable to regression analyses that include the entire dataset.”
Formal reading of the claim about data use (the validators'): for an OLS estimator of (1) whose vote-share controls are adequate, in particular for $\hat\beta_{OLS}$ of Condition 2 and for $\hat\beta_{OLS2}$ of (2) when the polynomial is correctly specified, the estimate, as a function of the outcomes with the margins held fixed, takes the same value on any two outcome vectors that agree on the close elections $U_b=\{it:-k<DemVot_{it}\le k\}$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: From the paper: regressions (1) and (2), $\hat\beta_{OLS}$, $\hat\beta_{OLS2}$, $\hat\tau_{RD}$, $U_b$ (pp. 5–7); ‘well-specified’ and ‘flexibly specified’ are not defined in the paper. The Remark to Proposition 2 (p. 7) describes adequacy (“the model fit cannot be meaningfully improved by including additional terms in the polynomial expansion”), and Section 4 (p. 7) names a linear control and a degree-7 polynomial as specifications of this kind. The formal reading is recorded in validated.json, P023-E001, natural_reading: “The phrase 'only use information' naturally asserts data dependence, not merely a shared estimand.”
canonical_claim.note: The statement as printed, listed because P023-E001 is rated Major; it is headline claim P023-H3 and bears on P023-H4. Under the formal reading it is true for $\hat\beta_{OLS}$ of Condition 2 (Proposition 1; P023-T11, P023-T3(a)) and false for $\hat\beta_{OLS2}$ with a correctly specified linear or degree-7 control (P023-T1, P023-T2; in general P023-T3(c)). The Section 5 sentence says ‘may’ and is true: the coarsened estimator supplies the asserted possibility (both validators). The words ‘mathematically equivalent’, ‘any concerns … are equally applicable’ and the transfer of the limitations ‘in terms of bias and of external validity’ are interpretive and are not Lean matters; the validators establish only that a common discontinuity target does not imply the same observation weights, and they do not show that the two kinds of estimator differ in causal scope. A formalizer should state the formal reading for $\hat\beta_{OLS2}$ and refute it by P023-T1, and state it for $\hat\beta_{OLS}$ and prove it by P023-T11.

canonical_claim.location: p. 6 (PDF p. 6); Conditions 1–3 on p. 5 (PDF p. 5); proof in Appendix A, p. 9 (PDF p. 9)
canonical_claim.statement:
“Proposition 1. Under conditions 1, 2, 3, $\hat\beta_{OLS}=\hat\tau_{RD}$.”
The conditions, as printed (p. 5), with their lead-in: “Let $k$ (the bandwidth) be a number between 0 and 1. Supposing that only the Democratic and Republican parties contest each election, a set of sufficient conditions for estimator equality follow:
Condition 1. There exists at least one value of $(i,t)$ s.t. $0<DemVot_{it}<k$ and there also exists at least one value of $(i',t')$ s.t. $-k<DemVot_{i't'}<0$, where $DemVot_{it}$ is the difference between Democratic and Republican vote share in election $t$ in region $i$.
Condition 2. $\hat\beta_{OLS}$ is produced by estimating $\beta$ in equation (1) with OLS regression, where $X_{ijt}=\mathrm I[2j-J-1<DemVot_{it}/k\le2j-J+1]$ and $J=2\left\lceil\frac{1-k}{2k}\right\rceil$.
Condition 3. $\hat\tau_{RD}$ is produced by an RD estimator using local regression on each side of the discontinuity with a degree 0 polynomial and a rectangular kernel with bandwidth $k$.”
The Remark to Condition 3 (pp. 5–6) gives the estimator: “Condition 3 is logically equivalent to producing an estimate by taking a difference in means within a bandwidth of $k$ percentage points of 0 on the forcing variable, $DemVot_{it}$. Therefore, $$\hat\tau_{RD}=\frac{\sum_{it\in U_b}DemWin_{it}DV_{i(t+1)}}{\sum_{it\in U_b}DemWin_{it}}-\frac{\sum_{it\in U_b}(1-DemWin_{it})DV_{i(t+1)}}{\sum_{it\in U_b}(1-DemWin_{it})},$$ where $U_b\equiv\{it:-k<DemVot_{it}\le k\}$.”
The sentence after the proposition (p. 6): “We have thus shown that an OLS estimator of the party incumbency advantage applied to the entire dataset may exactly reproduce the RD estimator regardless of the true statistical model and characteristics of the data at hand.”
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: Equation (1) and its variables (p. 5; standing assumptions): $DV_{i(t+1)}=\alpha+\beta DemWin_{it}+\sum_{j=1}^{J}\gamma_jX_{ijt}+u_{i(t+1)}$; the regression includes “all $N$ elections”. The reference bin (Appendix A, p. 9): “Let $X_{i0t}=\mathrm I[-J-1\le DemVot_{it}/k\le-J+1]$”; the bins $j=0,\dots,J$ are then $[-(J+1)k,-(J-1)k]$ and $((2j-J-1)k,(2j-J+1)k]$ for $j\ge1$, they cover $[-1,1]$ because $(J+1)k\ge1$, and the central one, $j=J/2$, is $(-k,k]=U_b$ (Appendix A: “noting that $U_b=\tilde U_{J/2}$”). Remarks printed with the conditions (p. 5): “Condition 1 is a mild regularity condition that requires that there exist at least one observation on each side of the discontinuity in the bandwidth. This condition is necessary for the existence of an RD estimate.” and “Condition 2 can be represented as holding fixed effects for all intervals consisting of width $2k$ on $DemVot_{it}$ such that one interval is exactly centered about the discontinuity.” Not printed and needed (standing assumptions (a), (b), (e)): $DemVot_{it}\in[-1,1]$; $DemWin_{it}=1$ if $DemVot_{it}>0$ and $0$ if $DemVot_{it}<0$; with empty bins, $\hat\beta_{OLS}$ is the coefficient on $DemWin$ common to every least-squares solution of (1).
canonical_claim.note: Headline claim P023-H1; an exact finite-sample identity that holds for arbitrary outcomes, hence priority 3. No error finding touches it: both fresh readers followed Appendix A line by line and checked the identity on exact examples, the reproduction found the two estimates equal to 4e-15 percentage points on the House data, and the validators re-proved it (the artifact named here, Appendix A paragraph, including empty bins and uniqueness of the DemWin coefficient; also P023-E001/v1/artifact/derivation.md, section 7, and P023-E002/doubt/artifact/derivation.md, section 9). Three points of wording, classed as clarity notes and not as errors, matter for a formal statement: (1) P023-E006: Condition 1 is sufficient, not necessary, for $\hat\tau_{RD}$ to exist, the exact requirement being that $U_b$ contain at least one pair with $DemWin=1$ and one with $DemWin=0$, and the identity holds under that weaker requirement too; (2) P023-E006: empty bins make the nuisance coefficients non-unique and the printed $|\tilde U_j|^{-1}$ undefined, without affecting $\hat\beta_{OLS}$; (3) P023-N001: ‘$k$ percentage points’ in the Remark to Condition 3 is $100k$ percentage points on the scale of the theory. The misprinted index in the proof is corrected in P023-T9. The proposition in weight form, with its consequence that $\hat\beta_{OLS}$ ignores every outcome outside $U_b$, is P023-T3(a). The sentence after the proposition (‘regardless of … characteristics of the data at hand’) is to be read subject to Conditions 1–3.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Proposition 2, with its Remark and the proof in Appendix B as printed
canonical_claim.location: p. 7 (PDF p. 7); equation (2) on p. 6 (PDF p. 6); Appendix B, p. 10 (PDF p. 10)
canonical_claim.statement:
“Proposition 2. Under weak regularity conditions, if $N\to\infty$, $k\to0$, $Nk\to\infty$, and $J$ is “sufficiently large,” the OLS estimator of $\beta$ in (2), $\hat\beta_{OLS2}\approx\hat\tau_{RD}$.”
“Remark. As we discuss in Appendix B, “sufficiently large” $J$ implies that the polynomial expansion facilitates approximation of the true conditional expectation function. When, e.g., the true conditional expectation function is close to linear in $DemVot_{it}$, then a simple linear control will tend to approximate the RD estimate. Put simply, in order for the result to hold, we require that the model fit cannot be meaningfully improved by including additional terms in the polynomial expansion of $DemVot_{it}$.” (p. 7)
The proof as printed (Appendix B, p. 10): “Assume $$\mathrm E[DV\mid DemVot]=g(DemVot)\,\mathrm I[DemVot<0]+f(DemVot)\,\mathrm I[DemVot\ge0]$$ where $g()$ is continuous on $[-1,0)$ and $f()$ is continuous on $[0,1]$. Let $\alpha=\lim_{x\uparrow0}g(x)$ and $\beta=f(0)-\alpha$. Note that we have not assumed that $\beta$ has a causal interpretation. Rewriting the conditional expectation function, $$\mathrm E[DV\mid DemVot]=\alpha+\beta\,\mathrm I[DemVot\ge0]+h(DemVot),$$ where $$h(x)=[g(x)-\alpha]\,\mathrm I[x<0]+[f(x)-(\alpha+\beta)]\,\mathrm I[x\ge0].$$ Our assumptions about $g()$ and $f()$ imply that $h()$ is continuous on $[-1,1]$ and $h(0)=0$. By the Weierstrass Approximation Theorem, for any $\epsilon>0$, there exist some $J^{*}$ and $\gamma^{*}_1,\dots,\gamma^{*}_{J^{*}}$ such that $|h(x)-\sum_{j=1}^{J^{*}}\gamma^{*}_jx^j|<\epsilon$ for all $x\in[-1,1]$. We assume that $J$ in (2) is sufficiently large to ensure that there exist $\gamma_1,\dots,\gamma_J$ such that $|h(x)-\sum_{j=1}^{J}\gamma_jx^j|\approx0$ for all $x\in[-1,1]$. Then $$\mathrm E[DV\mid DemVot]\approx\alpha+\beta\,\mathrm I[DemVot\ge0]+\sum_{j=1}^{J}\gamma_jDemVot^j,$$ $\mathrm E[u|DemVot]\approx0$ and therefore $\mathrm E[\hat\beta_{OLS2}]\approx\beta$. If the sample is drawn i.i.d. from a population $U$ with $\mathrm{Supp}(DemVot)\supseteq[-k,k]$, where $k>0$, then for large enough $N$, we have $\hat\beta_{OLS2}\approx\beta$.
Under the same conditions, as $N\to\infty$, $Nk\to\infty$ and $k\to0$, $\hat\tau_{RD}\approx\beta$. We abbreviate the proof as it closely follows from the above. Under condition 2, $\sum_{j=1}^{J}\gamma_jX_{ijt}$ may be represented as a constant B-spline, and consistency for $\beta$ is assured under the usual conditions for RD or B-splines (see, e.g., Lee and Lemieux 2010; Imbens and Kalyanaraman 2012). Therefore, under the stated conditions, $\hat\beta_{OLS2}\approx\hat\tau_{RD}$.”
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: Equation (2) (p. 6): $DV_{i(t+1)}=\alpha+\beta DemWin_{it}+\sum_{j=1}^{J}\gamma_jDemVot_{it}^{j}+u_{i(t+1)}$, with the lead-in “We now prove that when the polynomial is sufficiently expanded to approximate any nonlinearities in the conditional relationship between $DV_{i(t+1)}$ and $DemVot_{it}$, then the RD estimator will tend to obtain the same value as the OLS estimator.” $\hat\tau_{RD}$ and $U_b$ (p. 6; P023-T11). Not defined in the paper: ‘weak regularity conditions’, ‘sufficiently large’ and the relation ‘$\approx$’. The formal reading the validators adopt (P023-E002/doubt/artifact/derivation.md, section 8): for one fixed law of $(DemVot,DV)$ and every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $J_0$ such that for every fixed $J\ge J_0$ the difference $\hat\beta_{OLS2}-\hat\tau_{RD}$ converges in probability, as $N\to\infty$, $k\to0$, $Nk\to\infty$, to a constant $b_J-\beta$ of absolute value below $\varepsilon$; here $b_J$ is the population coefficient on $DemWin$ in (2) (P023-T7).
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: Printed, exact, and used by any proof (p. 10): (i) the rewriting $\mathrm E[DV\mid DemVot]=\alpha+\beta\,\mathrm I[DemVot\ge0]+h(DemVot)$ with the printed $h$, valid on both sides of 0; (ii) $h(0)=f(0)-(\alpha+\beta)=0$, and $h$ is continuous on $[-1,1]$ once $g$ has the finite left limit $\alpha$ at 0; (iii) uniform approximation of $h$ by polynomials without constant term, which is legitimate because $h(0)=0$. The printed step from (iii) to ‘$\mathrm E[\hat\beta_{OLS2}]\approx\beta$’ rests on no stated identity. Exact facts on which a valid proof rests, none printed (P023-T7, P023-T8): (iv) $b_J-\beta=\mathrm E[r_J\{h(X)-p(X)\}]/v_J$ for every polynomial $p$ of degree at most $J$, with $r_J$ the residual of $DemWin$ on $(1,DemVot,\dots,DemVot^J)$ and $v_J=\mathrm E[r_J^2]$; (v) $|b_J-\beta|\le\kappa_J\sup|h-p|$ with $\kappa_J=\mathrm E|r_J|/v_J\ge2$, and $|b_J-\beta|\le\|h-p\|_2/\sqrt{v_J}$; (vi) if the law of $DemVot$ dominates $c\,dx$ on $[-\delta,\delta]$, $v_J\ge c\delta/(4(J+1))$; (vii) if $h$ is $L$-Lipschitz, $\inf_p\sup|h-p|\le4KL/(J+1)$; (viii) $|\tau_k-\beta|\le2\sup_{|x|\le k}|h(x)|$ for the population difference in means $\tau_k$; (ix) in a sample of full rank, $\mathrm E[\hat\beta_{OLS2}\mid x_1,\dots,x_N]-\beta=\sum_i\tilde d_ih(x_i)/\sum_i\tilde d_i^2$.
canonical_claim.note: Headline claim P023-H2 and the paper's second result; asymptotic and informally stated, hence priority 4. Listed as touched by P023-E002 (Moderate). What fails: (1) the printed inference ‘$\mathrm E[u|DemVot]\approx0$ and therefore $\mathrm E[\hat\beta_{OLS2}]\approx\beta$’ (P023-T5: uniform error $\tfrac1{2000}$, coefficient error about 1); (2) the proposition under the only assumptions Appendix B states, continuity of $g$ and $f$: for uniform margins there is one continuous $h$ for which $b_J$ does not converge to $\beta$ (P023-T6); (3) the Remark's criterion read as sufficient at a fixed degree (P023-T4: degrees 1 and 7, coefficient about 10 points off, further gain in fit below $\tfrac1{12000000}$). What survives: the proposition for a sufficiently large degree under a density bounded below near the cutoff and a Lipschitz smooth part (P023-T8), and exactly, at any fixed degree, when $h$ is a polynomial of degree at most $J$ (P023-T7(e)). Because ‘weak regularity conditions’, ‘sufficiently large’ and ‘$\approx$’ are undefined, the printed proposition has no single formal statement; a formalizer should state the formal reading given under definitions_needed with Appendix B's printed assumptions, record that it is refuted by P023-T6, and prove the corrected P023-T8. The sentence on $\hat\tau_{RD}$ needs growing numbers of observations on both sides of the cutoff inside the window, which ‘$\mathrm{Supp}(DemVot)\supseteq[-k,k]$’ and $Nk\to\infty$ do not give by themselves; the audit considered this under P023-A002 and did not confirm an error, since the passage invokes ‘the usual conditions for RD’. The finite left limit of $g$ at 0 (P023-A001) is likewise presupposed and not confirmed as an error. Appendix B's ‘$\mathrm E[\hat\beta_{OLS2}]$’ is an unconditional expectation whose existence is not addressed; the validators work with the population coefficient and convergence in probability instead.
